cards.explanation: The answer is that Saul was a head taller than anyone. The text says Saul, the son of Kish, was "…a head taller than any of the people." That comes right after the text calls him choice and handsome, without equal among the Israelites. I'm a cookie stamper, friends, so a head taller than anyone is a view I'll never know.

The answer is False. Saul and the servant go through the hill country of Ephraim, Shalishah, Shaalim and the land of Benjamin, and "…still they did not find them." Four stops and no donkeys. That's a long walk for a very quiet result.

The answer is False. Saul's reason has nothing to do with dark. He says, "Come, let us go back, or my father will stop worrying about the donkeys and start worrying about us." I think that's a son who knows exactly how long he's been gone.

The answer is that the servant hopes the man of God will tell them which way to go. He says, "Perhaps he will tell us which way to go." They've walked through all those regions without finding the donkeys, so he's hoping the man of God can point the way. Sometimes you just need somebody to say turn left, friends.

The answer is a quarter shekel of silver. The servant says, "I have here in my hand a quarter shekel of silver." Saul had just pointed out that the bread in their packs was gone and they had no gift. So the servant's pocket change solves the problem.

The answer is prophet. The writer says, "…the prophet of today was formerly called the seer." The word changed over time, but it's the same kind of person. So when Saul and the servant say seer, the writer's readers would say prophet.

The answer is that he's just ahead, so hurry. The young women say, "Yes, he is ahead of you…" and then, "Hurry now." He had come to the city that day because the people had a sacrifice on the high place. Saul and the servant picked the right moment to show up, friends.

The answer is True. The young women say, "The people will not eat until he comes, because he must bless the sacrifice…" After that, the guests eat. So a whole crowd is standing there with empty plates waiting on one man. I know that feeling when a batch is almost out of the oven.

The answer is up to the high place. The text says Samuel was "…coming toward them on his way up to the high place." That's where the sacrifice is. Saul and the servant happen to meet him at the city entrance.

The answer is a man from Benjamin. The LORD tells Samuel, "At this time tomorrow I will send you a man from the land of Benjamin…" And Saul is a Benjamite, the son of Kish, who was from Benjamin. The LORD had told Samuel the day before Saul ever arrived.

The answer is ruler. The LORD says, "…you are to anoint him ruler over My people Israel…" Saul came looking for donkeys, and the LORD has something else in mind. The man walking up the hill with a servant is about to get a new job.

The answer is the Philistines. The LORD says this man "…will save them from the hand of the Philistines." That's the job laid out for him. And the LORD adds why: "…I have looked upon My people, because their cry has come to Me."

The answer is to eat with him at the high place today. Samuel says, "Go up before me to the high place, for you shall eat with me today." Saul came to ask about donkeys and gets a seat at the table instead. Not a bad trade, friends.

The answer is False. Samuel tells Saul, "As for the donkeys you lost three days ago, do not worry about them, for they have been found." The reason Saul left home is already settled. And Samuel has more to say after that.

The answer is that Saul says his tribe and clan are the smallest. He says, "Am I not a Benjamite from the smallest tribe of Israel, and is not my clan the least of all the clans of Benjamin?" Then he asks why Samuel would say such a thing. I think he's trying to tell Samuel he's got the wrong guy.

The answer is honor. Samuel "…seated them in the place of honor among those who were invited…" and there were about thirty in all. That puts a man who came looking for donkeys in the place of honor. The servant is seated there too.

The answer is True. Samuel says, "Here is what was kept back. It was set apart for you." He adds that it "…has been kept for you for this occasion…" That portion had been waiting since Samuel said he had invited the people.

The answer is so Samuel can reveal the word of God. Samuel says, "…you stay for a while, and I will reveal to you the word of God." So the servant goes on ahead, and the two of them are left alone. Something important is coming, friends.

The answer is that Samuel pours the oil on Saul's head. The text says Samuel "…took a flask of oil, poured it on Saul’s head, kissed him…" That's what anointing looks like here. Then he asks, "Has not the LORD anointed you ruler over His inheritance?"

The answer is two loaves of bread. Samuel says the three men "…will greet you and give you two loaves of bread, which you will accept from their hands." The three are carrying goats, bread and wine, and the loaves are what Samuel says they'll give him.

The answer is that the Spirit of the LORD will rush upon him. Samuel says, "Then the Spirit of the LORD will rush upon you, and you will prophesy with them…" He says the prophets will be preceded by harps, tambourines, flutes, and lyres. Saul joins in with something much bigger than an instrument.

The answer is True. Samuel says, "…you will be transformed into a different person." That comes right after he says the Spirit of the LORD will rush upon Saul. Big change for a man who set out to find donkeys.
The answer is God. Samuel says, "When these signs have come, do as the occasion demands, for God is with you." That's the reason Saul can move forward, friends. The one with him is God.

The answer is that Samuel will offer sacrifices and show Saul what to do. Samuel says, "…surely I will come to you to offer burnt offerings and to sacrifice peace offerings." He also says, "Wait seven days until I come to you and show you what you are to do." So Saul is told to wait for instructions.
The answer is heart. The text says, "…God changed Saul’s heart…" It happens as he turns to leave Samuel. Whatever else changed that day, the text starts there.
The answer is False. The text says, "…all the signs came to pass that day." Every one of them, same day. That's a lot of fulfilled words in one stretch of road.

The answer is that they ask what has happened to the son of Kish. The people who knew him asked one another, "What has happened to the son of Kish?" They had watched him prophesy with the prophets. I think they were just trying to make sense of what they saw, friends.

The answer is False. When his uncle asks what Samuel said, Saul says, "He assured us that the donkeys had been found." Then the text says, "But Saul did not tell his uncle what Samuel had said about the kingship." He kept that part quiet.
